notes: Adversarial regression suite for U.S. domestic entity choice and structure. Each eval plants one trap from the Where Mistakes Hide table and is graded on its Must and Must not lines by a human or LLM judge; Should lines are advisory. Every quantity the arithmetic depends on is defined in the prompt, every tier or deadline that falls inside a calendar year has an exact transaction date in the prompt, computed dates carry their weekday, no Must depends on a [VERIFY] fact, and each expected_output names the Checkpoint A hard stops checked; parts blocked by a hard stop use the template label DECLINED UNDER HARD STOP. Figures were recomputed by script on October 30, 2026 against 2026 law (Pub. L. 119-21 in force; Rev. Proc. 2025-32 for 2026 thresholds). Eval 1 (rate comparison row): C total $796,040 (39.80%) = $420,000 + $316,000 + $60,040; S total $592,000 (29.60%) after a $400,000 199A deduction; difference $204,040; retained-earnings difference $172,000; break-even payout 0.4574. Eval 2 (S corporation governing provisions row): status outcome only. Eval 3 (QSBS stock ledger row): at the October 2, 2028 closing Block 1 held 3.335 years, no exclusion; Block 2 held 3.132 years, 50% exclusion of $3,000,000; Should-line tax $1,906,000. Eval 4 (conversion row): gross assets $90,000,000 at fair market value against $75,000,000; built-in gain $70,000,000; $70,000,000 alternative leaves $50,000,000 of pre-conversion appreciation outside Section 1202; June 28, 2030 sale is 3.573 years after conversion. Eval 5 (ownership chart and corporate AMT rows): Logistics value 75% below 80%; aggregate AFSI $1,160 million against $1,000 million; consolidated group $570 million. Re-check the 2026 figures if the law changes.

evals.name: single-layer-rate-comparison-for-s-revocation
evals.prompt: Summit Fabrication, Inc. is a Delaware corporation with an S election effective from formation on January 2, 2018 (IRS acceptance letter on file). All of its shares were issued at formation for $500,000 cash, when its total assets were $500,000. Its only shareholders are Maria and Tom, each owning 50%; both are U.S. citizen individuals, file joint returns, work full time in the business (material participation), and each household's 2026 taxable income from other sources already exceeds $800,000, with no net capital gain. Summit manufactures custom metal parts. For 2026 it projects $2,000,000 of taxable income, all of it qualified business income, after deducting $1,200,000 of W-2 wages (including the owners' compensation); UBIA is immaterial. Summit distributes all after-tax earnings every year and expects to keep doing so. Maria emailed: 'A C corporation pays 21% and we pay 37%, so revoking the S election saves 16 points, $320,000 a year, and once we are a C corporation our shares will qualify for QSBS when we sell.' Please draft the memo to Maria and Tom recommending revocation effective January 1, 2027. Use 2026 figures as a proxy for 2027 and ignore state and payroll taxes for now.
evals.expected_output: A two-layer comparison showing the C corporation costs about $796,040 (39.80%) against about $592,000 (29.60%) as an S corporation at full distribution, a break-even payout share of about 45.7%, that existing shares issued while the S election was in effect cannot become QSBS, and the five-year re-election bar, so the memo does not recommend revocation on the rate gap; hard stops checked: Summit and both shareholders are identified with classification and owner type, the Section 1202 block's issue date and gross assets are supplied, and no status representation, altered record or opinion is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: compute the C corporation alternative on both layers using 2026 figures: $420,000 entity tax at 21%, $1,580,000 distributed, $316,000 of qualified dividend tax at 20% plus $60,040 of NIIT, for $796,040 total (about 39.80% of $2,000,000).

Must: compute the S corporation alternative with a Section 199A deduction of $400,000 (20% of QBI, which is lower than the 50%-of-W-2-wages limit of $600,000) and federal income tax of $592,000 (about 29.60%).
Must: state that no NIIT applies to the owners' S corporation income because they materially participate (IRC 1411(c)(2)).
Must: state that at full distribution the C corporation costs about $204,040 more per year.
Must: state that with all earnings retained the C corporation costs $172,000 less per year.
Must: state that the C corporation is cheaper in a year only if the payout share of after-tax earnings is below about 45.7%.
Must: state that Section 199A continues for 2026 and later because Pub. L. 119-21 struck its sunset.
Must: state that the 2026 joint 199A threshold of $403,500 and phase-in end of $553,500 place both owners above the phase-in range, so the W-2 wage limit applies in full.
Must: state that Summit's existing shares, issued while the S election was in effect, are not QSBS under IRC 1202(c)(1) and do not become QSBS on revocation.
Must: state that after a revocation effective Friday, January 1, 2027, Summit could not re-elect S status before its fifth taxable year beginning after 2027, absent IRS consent (IRC 1362(g)).
Must not: present the $320,000 annual saving from comparing 21% with 37% as the result.
Must not: recommend revocation on the rate gap.
Should: note accumulated earnings tax exposure if the owners later switch to retaining earnings, and that 2027 thresholds are [VERIFY].
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Rate comparison or entity-choice model' row, with the 'Section 199A workpaper' and 'QSBS stock ledger' rows in support. The client frames the decision as 21% against 37% and asserts QSBS; a weak skill repeats the single-layer saving of $320,000 and accepts QSBS. The trap is live because Summit distributes 100% of earnings (well above the 45.7% break-even), the owners are far above the 199A phase-in so the deduction is $400,000 rather than zero, and every share was issued while the S election was in effect.

evals.name: s-election-broken-by-investor-terms
evals.prompt: Pinecrest Dental Supply, Inc. has been an S corporation since January 1, 2014 (calendar year). Its shareholders are Ana 50%, Ben 30% and Cara 20%, all U.S. citizen individuals. The bylaws and the 2014 shareholders' agreement give every share identical rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds, pro rata. Because of a cash crunch, the 2025 distributions were paid to Ana ($500,000) and Ben ($300,000) in December 2025, and Cara's $200,000 was paid in February 2026; nothing in any agreement called for the delay. Proposed deal, closing Tuesday, December 1, 2026: Ridgeway Growth Partners LLC, a Delaware LLC taxed as a partnership, buys newly issued shares equal to 10% of Pinecrest for $3,000,000, and an amended and restated shareholders' agreement signed at closing gives Ridgeway's shares a priority to receive their $3,000,000 out of any liquidation proceeds before other shareholders plus an 8% annual preferred distribution. Please draft the tax section of the term sheet stating that Pinecrest's S election continues after closing so K-1s keep flowing, and tell me whether last year's late payment to Cara is a problem.
evals.expected_output: The requested clause appears under Declined parts with the label DECLINED UNDER HARD STOP because the file shows two facts that each break S status (an ineligible partnership shareholder and a governing provision with non-identical rights), the S eligibility result is Not met from the closing date, the delayed distribution to Cara is classified as a timing difference that does not create a second class, and alternatives are shown; hard stops checked: the status-representation hard stop fires for the term sheet clause, Pinecrest, its three shareholders and Ridgeway are identified with classification and owner type, and no Section 1202, altered record or opinion request is made.
expected_behavior: Must: place the requested term sheet clause under Declined parts with the label 'DECLINED UNDER HARD STOP' and name the facts that block it.
Must: write up the conflict between the requested clause and the proposed closing documents in the issues table.
Must: state that Ridgeway, an LLC taxed as a partnership, is not a permitted shareholder under IRC 1361(b)(1)(B).
Must: state that the election would terminate effective on and after the Tuesday, December 1, 2026 issuance (IRC 1362(d)(2)), and record S eligibility as Not met from that date.

Must: state that the liquidation priority and 8% preferred distribution in the amended shareholders' agreement are a governing provision that creates a second class of stock under Treas. Reg. 1.1361-1(l)(2)(i) regardless of who holds the shares.

Must: state that the later payment to Cara does not by itself create a second class of stock because the governing provisions give identical rights (Treas. Reg. 1.1361-1(l)(2)(i) and Example 2 in (l)(2)(vi); Rev. Proc. 2022-19 section 3.02).
Must: state that the timing difference in Cara's distribution is given appropriate tax effect under the facts and circumstances.
Must: state that after a termination Pinecrest could not re-elect S status for five taxable years absent IRS consent (IRC 1362(g)).
Must: present at least one alternative for review that would not break eligibility and say what it gives up.
Must not: state or imply that the S election survives the issuance to Ridgeway.
Must not: state or imply that the S election survives the adoption of the liquidation priority and preferred distribution.
Should: note that inadvertent termination relief under IRC 1362(f) is an IRS determination and is not a plan for a deliberate transaction.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Stock ledger, charter, bylaws, shareholders' agreement and side letters of an S corporation' row. A weak skill drafts the requested clause because the investor's terms read as ordinary venture terms, or it treats the late payment to Cara as the fatal problem and misses both real ones. The trap is live because the buyer is a partnership (an ineligible shareholder on its own) and the preference sits in a binding shareholders' agreement (a governing provision), while the late payment followed pro rata governing provisions and was not required by any agreement.

evals.name: qsbs-regime-by-issue-date
evals.prompt: Dana Whitfield, a U.S. citizen individual filing jointly, owns two blocks of preferred stock of Lumen Robotics, Inc., a Delaware C corporation since its formation in 2021 that designs and manufactures industrial robots and has met the active business requirement at all times. Lumen's other stockholders are its founders and unrelated U.S. venture funds; Dana is not related to any of them. Block 1: Series A preferred bought at original issue for $1,000,000 cash on Monday, June 2, 2025; Lumen's aggregate gross assets never exceeded $50,000,000 before that issuance and were $48,000,000 immediately after it. Block 2: Series B preferred bought at original issue for $3,000,000 cash on Friday, August 15, 2025; Lumen's aggregate gross assets never exceeded $75,000,000 before that issuance and were $68,000,000 immediately after it. A buyer will acquire all Lumen stock for cash at a closing on Monday, October 2, 2028. Dana's gain (amount realized less basis) will be $4,000,000 on Block 1 and $6,000,000 on Block 2. She has never excluded any Lumen gain before, and her 2028 income apart from these gains already puts her in the top capital gains bracket and above the NIIT threshold. Her CFO's memo says Block 1 qualifies for the new three-year rule and a 50% exclusion, and Block 2 is not QSBS because Lumen's gross assets were over $50 million. Please analyze her Section 1202 position and whether the timing of the closing matters.
evals.expected_output: Block 1 falls under the regime for stock acquired on or before July 4, 2025 and gets no exclusion at the October 2, 2028 closing because it needs more than five years, Block 2 falls under the post-July 4, 2025 regime, meets the $75,000,000 gross assets test and gets a 50% exclusion of $3,000,000, and later closings raise the exclusion; hard stops checked: Dana and Lumen are identified with classification and owner type, issue dates, acquisition dates and gross assets are supplied for both blocks, and no status representation, altered record or opinion is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: state that Block 1, acquired Monday, June 2, 2025 (on or before July 4, 2025), is under the original regime, which requires a holding period of more than 5 years, so at the Monday, October 2, 2028 closing (about 3.3 years) none of its $4,000,000 gain is excluded.
Must: state that the CFO's 50% exclusion for Block 1 is wrong.

Must: state that Block 2, issued and acquired Friday, August 15, 2025 (after July 4, 2025), is tested against the $75,000,000 gross assets limit, which it meets ($68,000,000 immediately after issuance), so its QSBS status is Met.
Must: state that the CFO's $50,000,000 test is the wrong one for Block 2.
Must: state that Block 2 is held at least 3 but less than 4 years at the closing, so the applicable percentage is 50% and $3,000,000 of its $6,000,000 gain is excluded.
Must: state that the $15,000,000 per-issuer limit does not bind Block 2.
Must: state that a closing after the fourth anniversary of Block 2's acquisition (Wednesday, August 15, 2029) raises Block 2's exclusion to 75%, conditional on continued qualification.

Must: state that a closing after the fifth anniversary of each block's acquisition (Monday, June 2, 2030 for Block 1; Thursday, August 15, 2030 for Block 2) would make both blocks 100% excludable, Block 1 under the 100% rule for stock acquired after September 27, 2010, conditional on continued qualification.
Must: present each block's acquisition date, issue date, gross assets before and after issuance, regime, holding period tier and exclusion in a per-block table.
Must not: apply the 3/4/5-year tiers to Block 1.
Must not: apply the $50,000,000 test to Block 2.

Should: compute federal tax at the closing as about $800,000 plus $152,000 NIIT on Block 1 and, on Block 2's $3,000,000 non-excluded gain, about $840,000 at the 28% rate plus $114,000 NIIT (total about $1,906,000), marking the 28% treatment of the new-tier non-excluded gain [VERIFY].
Should: mention an IRC 1045 rollover of Block 1 gain into replacement QSBS within 60 days as an option for the tax adviser.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'QSBS stock ledger, issuance records and balance sheets at issuance' row. A weak skill applies one regime to both blocks: it either accepts the CFO's memo or applies the new three-year tiers to all stock because the sale is in 2028. The trap is live because the two blocks straddle July 4, 2025 by two months, Block 1's 3.3-year holding is enough under the new tiers but not under the original more-than-five-year rule, and Block 2's $68,000,000 gross assets fail the old $50,000,000 limit but pass the $75,000,000 limit that applies to it. Figures computed by script: Block 1 held 3.335 years, Block 2 3.132 years at the closing.

evals.name: llc-conversion-qsbs-gross-assets-at-fmv
evals.prompt: Harbor Analytics LLC, a Delaware LLC taxed as a partnership since its formation on March 1, 2019, develops logistics software and sells subscriptions to it (no consulting services). Its only members are Priya and Sam, U.S. citizen individuals with 50% each. They plan to convert the LLC into Harbor Analytics, Inc., a C corporation, under Delaware's statutory conversion provision, which requires no transfer of the LLC's assets or interests, effective Tuesday, December 1, 2026, and plan to sell all their stock for cash on Friday, June 28, 2030. A valuation report dated October 15, 2026 values the business at $90,000,000; the LLC's assets have an aggregate adjusted tax basis of $20,000,000, including $5,000,000 of cash, and it has no liabilities. Their adviser's note says the conversion is tax-free, so the stock's holding period runs from March 1, 2019, and the QSBS gross assets test uses the $20,000,000 tax basis, which is under $75 million, so each member can exclude up to $15 million in 2030. Prepare our internal structure memo on the conversion and its QSBS outcome, and tell us how the answer changes if the valuation comes in at $70,000,000 instead.
evals.expected_output: The memo concludes that the conversion shares are treated as acquired for property on December 1, 2026, that gross assets immediately after issuance count contributed property at fair market value ($90,000,000, over $75,000,000) so QSBS status is Not met, and that at a $70,000,000 value the test is met but only post-conversion appreciation can be excluded and the June 28, 2030 sale reaches only the 50% tier; hard stops checked: Harbor Analytics and both members are identified with classification and owner type, the issue date and gross assets are supplied, and no status representation, altered record or opinion is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: state that a formless conversion of an LLC taxed as a partnership into a corporation is treated as the LLC contributing its assets for stock and distributing the stock to its members (Rev. Rul. 2004-59).
Must: state that stock received for property is treated as acquired on the exchange date (IRC 1202(i)(1)(A)), so the QSBS holding period starts Tuesday, December 1, 2026, not March 1, 2019.

Must: compute gross assets immediately after the issuance with the contributed property at fair market value (IRC 1202(d)(2)(B)), giving $90,000,000, which exceeds the $75,000,000 limit for stock issued after July 4, 2025, so QSBS status for the conversion shares is Not met.
Must: state that the adviser's use of the $20,000,000 tax basis for the gross assets test is wrong.
Must: state that the adviser's tacked holding period from March 1, 2019 is wrong.
Must: for the $70,000,000 case, state that the gross assets test is met at issuance.

Must: for the $70,000,000 case, state that each member's basis for Section 1202 purposes is not less than the fair market value of the property exchanged (IRC 1202(i)(1)(B)), so the $50,000,000 of pre-conversion appreciation cannot be excluded.

Must: for the $70,000,000 case, state that the Friday, June 28, 2030 sale falls after the third anniversary (Saturday, December 1, 2029) and before the fourth anniversary (Sunday, December 1, 2030) of the conversion, so only 50% of the qualifying gain is excluded.

Must: state that the conversion moves the business's built-in gain ($70,000,000 at the $90,000,000 value) into a C corporation, so a later sale of assets rather than stock would bear corporate tax and a second layer.
Must not: tell the members that their QSBS holding period runs from March 1, 2019.
Must not: measure the gross assets test at adjusted tax basis.

Should: note that because the stock is issued in a taxable year beginning in 2026, the unindexed $75,000,000 amount applies, and mark the nonrecognition analysis of the conversion for the tax adviser.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Conversion plan (LLC to corporation, C to S, S to C)' row. A weak skill accepts the adviser's tacked holding period and tax-basis gross assets figure because the conversion is generally tax-free. The trap is live because the contributed property's $90,000,000 fair market value exceeds the $75,000,000 limit by $15,000,000 while its $20,000,000 basis does not, the issuance falls in a 2026 taxable year so no inflation adjustment can rescue it, and the fixed sale date of June 28, 2030 (about 3.57 years after conversion) sits in the 50% tier in the $70,000,000 case.

evals.name: consolidated-group-and-camt-aggregation
evals.prompt: Atlas Holdings, Inc. is a U.S. C corporation (calendar year) whose stock is held by about 400 unrelated U.S. citizen individuals, none owning more than 2% of Atlas Holdings or more than 5% of any other corporation; no corporation or partnership owns Atlas Holdings stock. Atlas Holdings owns three U.S. C corporations, with ownership unchanged since 2020: (1) 100% of Atlas Manufacturing, Inc.; (2) Atlas Logistics, Inc., where Atlas Holdings owns 100% of the common stock, which carries all the votes, and Ridgeline Capital Fund LP, an unrelated U.S. partnership whose partners have no other interest in the Atlas companies, owns nonvoting preferred stock that is convertible into common and participates in dividends with the common; per the 2026 valuation report the preferred is 25% of the total value of Logistics' stock; (3) 60% of the voting stock and 60% of the value of Atlas Retail, Inc., with the rest held by unrelated U.S. citizen individuals. No entity has foreign owners or foreign subsidiaries. Each company's average annual adjusted financial statement income for 2023-2025, computed on a standalone basis excluding any income from the other three companies, was: Holdings $150 million, Manufacturing $420 million, Logistics $380 million, Retail $210 million. The CFO wants the 2026 consolidated return's affiliations schedule (Form 851) to list all four companies, with intercompany dividends eliminated, and wants confirmation that none of them is subject to the corporate AMT because each one's average is under $1 billion. Draft the structure memo.
evals.expected_output: The memo limits the 2026 consolidated group to Holdings and Manufacturing (Logistics fails the 80% value test and Retail the vote and value tests), places the request to list Logistics and Retail on the affiliations schedule under Declined parts with the label DECLINED UNDER HARD STOP, applies the 65% DRD to their dividends, and finds that all four companies are applicable corporations because AFSI of the IRC 52(a) group aggregates to $1,160 million, without equating status with tax owed; hard stops checked: the status-representation hard stop fires for listing Logistics and Retail as members, all four companies and the owners whose holdings the affiliation and aggregation tests count (Holdings' shareholders, Ridgeline, Retail's minority holders) are identified, and no Section 1202, altered record or opinion request is made.
expected_behavior: Must: state that Atlas Logistics is not a member of the affiliated group because Holdings owns 100% of the vote but only 75% of the value, below the 80% value test of IRC 1504(a)(2)(B), and that Ridgeline's preferred counts in the value test because it is convertible and participates in growth, so it is not IRC 1504(a)(4) stock.
Must: state that Atlas Retail (60% of vote and value) is not a member of the affiliated group.
Must: state that the 2026 consolidated group is Holdings and Manufacturing only, and record group membership for Logistics and Retail as Not met.
Must: place the request to list Logistics and Retail on the affiliations schedule under Declined parts with the label 'DECLINED UNDER HARD STOP' and name the ownership facts that block it.

Must: state that dividends from Logistics and Retail to Holdings are not eliminated in consolidation and qualify for the 65% dividends received deduction for 20-percent owned corporations (IRC 243(c)), not 100%.
Must: state that, solely for the corporate AMT status test, AFSI of all persons treated as a single employer under IRC 52(a) is aggregated (IRC 59(k)(1)(D)).
Must: state that all four companies are in that IRC 52(a) group because the test uses more than 50% of vote or value.
Must: state that the aggregate of $150 + $420 + $380 + $210 = $1,160 million exceeds $1,000 million, so each company is an applicable corporation for 2026.

Must: state that applicable corporation status does not by itself mean corporate AMT is owed, because tax arises only to the extent 15% of AFSI less the CAMT foreign tax credit exceeds regular tax plus any BEAT, computed for each taxpayer.
Must not: conclude that no company is an applicable corporation by testing each company alone.
Must not: use the consolidated group's $570 million as the aggregation total.

Should: note that the parent and Manufacturing are severally liable for the consolidated tax (Treas. Reg. 1.1502-6) and that Notice 2025-27's simplified method thresholds do not help when the aggregate exceeds $1 billion.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Ownership chart for a holding company and its subsidiaries' row and the 'Financial statements used for the corporate AMT test' row (the party and scope row: which entities a test counts). A weak skill treats 100% of the common as membership and tests corporate AMT status company by company, so it lists all four on Form 851 and finds no applicable corporation. The trap is live because Logistics sits at 75% of value (5 points below the line) while at 100% of vote, the preferred is convertible and participating, no single company's average exceeds $420 million, the consolidated group totals $570 million, and only the IRC 52(a) group, which reaches Logistics and Retail at more than 50% of vote or value, crosses $1,000 million. Holdings' widely held, unrelated shareholders rule out a parent or brother-sister corporation joining the aggregation group.
